cognate: Gk ἱδρώς (*swid-ōs) / ἱδρόω ~ Ved. svéda- (*swoyd-o-) / √svid- (perf. ptc. siṣvidāná-): noun and verb both from *sweyd- 'sweat' in both traditions
drift_or_renewal: none in the core figure; Greek renews the verb as a denominative (ἱδρόω from the noun) where Vedic keeps the primary root verb; the Hippocratic instances shift the noun to the dative of manner (ἱδρῶτι ἱδρῶντες) in a clinical register
shared_syntax: figura etymologica: the noun 'sweat' as internal (cognate) accusative of the verb 'to sweat' — Il. 4.27 ἱδρῶ ... ἵδρωσα (relative clause, aorist), RV 10.106.10c svédam āsiṣvidānā́ (perfect participle, dual); Hippocratic prose has the same pairing with the noun in the dative
context: Both poetic instances are about exertion: Hera's 'sweat that I sweated with toil (μόγῳ), and my horses grew weary' while gathering the host; the Aśvins compared to ploughmen/farm labourers (kīnā́rā iva) 'having sweated sweat'. Vedic otherwise uses siṣvidāná- for the toiling worshipper (RV 4.2.6, 7.103.8). Corpus searches: this is the only noun+verb co-occurrence of the root in a Homeric line (32 lines with the root) and the only cognate-accusative instance in the RV (11 stanzas with svéda/√svid). Caveat: cognate accusative is productive in both languages, so the match may be independently generated; what is shared is the same lexeme in the same figure in the same toil context.

cognate: Gk ὀστέον ~ Lat. os, ossis ~ Ved. ásthi/asthán- (*h₃ésth₁); Gk νεῦρον ~ Lat. neruus ~ Ved. snā́van- (*snéh₁wr̥/-n-); the third member, Gk ἄρθρον ~ Lat. articulus, shares only the root *h₂er- 'fit' (different suffixes)
drift_or_renewal: Latin neruus has metathesis/remodelling of *snēwr̥ but the same sense 'sinew'; the 'joints' member is root-cognate only (ἄρθρον *h₂er-dʰro- vs articulus from artus *h₂r̥-tu-); Vedic has no joint member but adds marrow (majjan-) and vessels (dhamani-), cf. Lucretius' uenae
shared_syntax: coordinated enumeration of body tissues with both 'bones' and 'sinews' as members: ὀστέων καὶ νεύρων καὶ ἄρθρων (Vect. 42) ~ neruis atque ossibus articulisque (Lucr. 3.697), per neruos atque ossa (3.567); Vedic asthíbhyas ... snā́vabhyo in the same ablative list (AVŚ 2.33)
context: All three are body-inventory contexts: Hippocratic anatomy and surgery; Lucretius on the soul spread through and held by sinews and bones, and on death or a wound loosening them; the AV yakṣma charm driving disease out of each tissue (AVŚ 2.33, AVP 4.7) and the cosmogony of the body (AVŚ 11.8). The argument rests on the same two inherited words recurring as a coordinated pair in three branches, not on any marked poetics. Caveats: listing body tissues is generic and both words are the ordinary inherited terms; Lucretius may be following Greek medical or Epicurean vocabulary, so Latin independence is not assured; no Avestan bone+sinew pair turned up.

cognate: Gk χειμών / χεῖμα ~ Ved. híma- 'cold, winter' (~ Av. ziiā̊/zaiiana-) from *ǵʰeym-; the hot member is a *gʷʰer- 'warm' derivative in both Greek (θέρος) and Vedic (gharmá-, cf. ghraṃsá-)
drift_or_renewal: Gk θέρος has narrowed from 'heat' to 'summer' (cf. θερμός), while Ved. gharmá-/ghraṃsá- still mean 'heat'; Avestan renews the summer member with hąmina- (*sem-)
shared_syntax: two-member merism of the hot and cold season (καὶ χειμῶνος καὶ θέρεος; ghraṃsaḥ ... himaḥ), in Vedic also negated (na ghraṃs tatāpa na himo jaghāna AVŚ 7.18.3), cf. negated οὐδ' ... χείματος οὐδὲ θέρευς Od. 7.118
context: The pair stands for the whole cycle of the year: Hippocratic weather and season lore; AVŚ 13.1 makes heat and cold, set up by Rohita, the source of the sacrifice; AVŚ 7.18.3 (rain charm) and Od. 7.118 (Alcinous' orchard, fruit never failing) negate both seasons to say 'never'. Weak: a winter+summer pair is the obvious way to name the year, the only fully cognate member is the inherited word for winter, and the Vedic hot word is not the same derivative as θέρος.

note: Slab is almost all Hippocratic prose pivots with Cato, Lucretius and AV partners; most bundles share only common roots. 3 claims (2 medium, 1 low). Considered and dropped: μέλιτος γλυκίων ~ melle dulci dulcior (in the slab, γλυκύς goes with wine, not honey; the idea is universal), ἐν μέλιτι λείχειν ~ mel lingere (the contexts do not match), heel/forefoot (πτέρνη ~ pārṣṇi; anatomical only).
